newsitem.title: USA: Norfolk Southern offers new Conrail plan.
newsitem.headline: Norfolk Southern offers new Conrail plan.

text.p: Norfolk Southern Corp said it will buy 9.9 percent of outstanding shares of Conrail Inc at $115 each if Conrail shareholders defeat a key provision in the railroad's planned merger with CSX Corp.

Norfolk Southern said it would amend its existing all-cash tender offer to buy 8.2 million shares of Conrail, representing the maximum amount that could be purchased without triggering Conrail's anti-takeover defense plan.

The move by Norfolk Southern was the latest in a fierce battle for control of Conrail. Although Norfolk Southern has repeatedly offered more money for Conrail than CSX, Conrail has not strayed from its position that the planned union with CSX has more strategic benefits.
Norfolk Southern noted the 9.9 percent offer would not be subject to termination of the merger pact between Conrail and CSX and would not require any action by Conrail's board.
CSX plans to buy Conrail in a cash and stock transaction valued at about $9.1 billion. Norfolk Southern has offered to buy Conrail for about $10.3 billion in cash.

Shareholders are to vote Friday on a key provision that would let the planned transaction proceed. Conrail is asking investors to waive a Pennsylvania law that effectively requires CSX, which already owns 19.9 percent of Conrail shares, to pay $110 per share in cash for the rest.
If shareholders waive that provision, CSX will buy another 20 percent of Conrail shares for $110 per share and acquire the rest of Conrail in stock.

After buying 9.9 percent of Conrail, Norfolk Southern said it would begin a second all-cash tender offer for all the remaining Conrail common shares and ESOP preferred shares at $115 a share. Terms and conditions of that tender offer would essentially be unchanged from its current offer, Norfolk Southern said.

"Conrail shareholders have an opportunity to reassert control over their corporation and reject the coercive tactics being used to pressure them into approving CSX's inferior offer," Norfolk Southern chief executive officer David Goode said in a news release. (( --Robin Sidel, 212/859-1723))
